en: The Theravāda Vinaya:
Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga,
Pārājika Section
8. The Training Rule on the Eight Bases At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six bhikkhunīs, being lustful, [associated] with a lustful man.
They consent to being taken by the hand; they consent to being taken by the corner of the outer robe; they stand together; they converse;
they go to an appointment; they consent to a man’s approach; they enter a secluded place;
they expose their bodies for that purpose, for the sake of indulging in this unrighteous practice.
Those bhikkhunīs who were of few desires … [as above] … complained, grumbled, and were indignant, saying:
“How can the bhikkhunīs of the group of six, being lustful, consent to the grasping of the hands of a lustful man,
consent to the grasping of the corner of his outer robe, stand together with him, and converse with him?”
“They will even go to an appointment; they will consent to a man’s arrival; they will enter a secluded place;
they will even prepare their bodies for that purpose, for the sake of practicing this unrighteousness.
… “Is it true, monks, that the group-of-six bhikkhunīs, being lustful, [approached] a lustful man?”
Do they consent to being taken by the hand? Do they consent to being taken by the corner of the outer robe? Do they stand together? Do they converse?
Do they go to appointments? Do they consent to a man’s approach? Do they enter secluded places?
Do they expose their bodies for that purpose, for the sake of practicing this unrighteous conduct?”
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:
“… How indeed, monks, can the group-of-six bhikkhunīs, being lustful, [accept anything from] a lustful man?”
They will consent to being taken by the hand; they will consent to being taken by the corner of the outer robe;
they will stand together; they will converse; they will go to appointments; they will consent to the arrival of a man;
they will enter secluded places; and they will expose their bodies for that purpose, for the sake of practicing this unrighteous conduct.
“Monks, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And thus, monks, let the bhikkhunīs recite this training rule:
‘If a bhikkhunī who is lustful should consent to the grasping of the hand by a man who is lustful, [she commits an offense entailing expiation].’”
If she should consent to being taken by the corner of the outer robe, or should stand together [with a man], or should converse [with him], or should go to a rendezvous,
or should consent to a man’s coming to her, or should enter a concealed place,
or should arrange her body for that purpose in order to indulge in unrighteous conduct— this too is a *pārājika* offense involving exclusion from the community; it consists of eight bases.”
"But whichever" means whichever such...
"nun" means... [as before].
...pe... this is the "bhikkhunī" intended in this context.
"Lustful" means one who is infatuated, full of longing, and whose mind is bound [to another].
"One who is lustful" means one who is impassioned, full of longing, and whose mind is bound [to another].
"A person" means...
A human male, not a *yakkha*, not a *peta*, and not an animal, who is conscious and capable of engaging in physical contact.
"Or he consents to the grasping of the hand" (*hatthaggahaṇa*):
"hand" (*hattha*) means from the elbow down to the tips of the nails.
If, for the purpose of indulging in this unrighteous practice, she consents to being grasped above the collarbone or below the knees, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
Or, "if she consents to being grasped by the corner of the outer robe":
if, for the purpose of indulging in this unrighteous practice, she consents to being grasped while wearing or wrapped in her lower robe, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
"Or stands still":
if she stands within arm's reach of a man for the purpose of engaging in this unrighteous practice, there is an offense of *thullaccaya*.
"Or converses": [if she does so]...
If she converses while standing within arm’s reach of a man for the purpose of practicing this unrighteous practice, it is a *thullaccaya* offense.
“Or she goes to an appointment”:
if, having been told by a man, “Come to such-and-such a place,” she goes for the purpose of practicing this unrighteous practice, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for every step.
As soon as he has entered within arm’s reach of the man, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
“Or consents to a man approaching” means:
if she consents to a man approaching for the purpose of engaging in that which is not the true Dhamma, there is an offense of dukkaṭa.
As soon as he has entered within arm’s reach, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
Or, "should enter a concealed place":
as soon as he has entered any kind of concealed space for the purpose of practicing that unrighteous act, there is an offense of thullaccaya.
"Or she should apply her body for that purpose":
if, standing within arm's reach of a man, she applies her body for the sake of practicing that which is not the true Dhamma, there is an offense of thullaccaya. This also.
It is said with reference to the previous [cases].
"She becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense" means:

just as a palmyra tree whose crown is cut off is incapable of further growth, even so a bhikkhunī who fulfills the eighth ground becomes no longer a samaṇī, no longer a daughter of the Sakyans. Therefore it is said, "she becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense."
"Non-residence":
"Residence" means performing legal acts together, reciting the scriptures together, and training under the same rules. This is what is called residence.
That [residence] does not exist with her; therefore it is called "non-residence."
There is no offense if it was unintentional,
or if there was a lack of mindfulness.
For one who does not know,
for one who does not consent,
for one who is insane,
For one whose mind is distracted,
for one overwhelmed by pain,
and for one who is a first-time offender.
The fourth *pārājika* is finished.
Noble ladies, the eight *pārājika* rules have been recited.
Should a bhikkhunī commit any one or another of these, she does not obtain communion with the bhikkhunīs; as it was before, so it is after—she is *pārājika*, one who is no longer in communion.
In this matter, friends, I ask you:
"Are you pure in this?
A second time I ask: [the same].
“Are you pure in this matter?
A third time I ask:
“Are you pure in this matter?”
"Venerable ladies, this matter is pure; therefore, you are silent. Thus do I understand it.
The section on the offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*) in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga* is concluded.
